## MNIST handwriting recognition

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Famous example: USPS handwriting recognition system
  - Work of UB's Venu Govindaraju! [https://www.buffalo.edu/research/research-expertise/case-study-ai-at-usps.html](https://www.buffalo.edu/research/research-expertise/case-study-ai-at-usps.html)
- The MNIST database (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology) is a large collection of handwritten digits.
  - [https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/hojjatk/mnist-dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/hojjatk/mnist-dataset)
- Good lesson in data cleaning:
  - Starting point: 9,298 digits manually extracted from mail passing through Buffalo USPS in 1989. Human error rate: 2.5%! Messy data!
  - NIST database: separate training/test datasets sample from different populations, 16x16 black-and-white.
  - MNIST: better training/test sampling, 26x26, anti-aliased (greyscale).

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/pasted-movie.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Grid of MNIST handwritten digit samples: rows for digits 0 through 9, each row showing roughly 20 different handwritten variations of that digit as white strokes on black backgrounds."}

- MNIST digit images
![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide13_image12.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a convolutional neural network architecture processing a 28x28 MNIST digit image ('4'): two convolution+ReLU and max-pooling stages (32x28x28 to 32x14x14, then 64x14x14 to 64x7x7), flattened into a 3136-unit layer, a 128-unit dense layer, and a 10-unit output layer labeled 0-9."}

- MNIST convolutional neural network

# Basics

---

## Basics

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- Concepts behind neural networks are not particular deep
  - "Build a function out of many small functions"
- Nor are neural networks a particular new idea!
  - A very simple example: least squares regression (1795)
  - Perceptron [('58)](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0042519); multilayer perceptrons+stochastic gradient descent (['67](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/amari1967.pdf)); backpropagation ('70/80s); recurrent/convolutional NNs ('80/90s)
- Why are we only experience the ML revolution now, in 2026?
  - Free availability of large datasets of labeled data
  - Free availability of open source languages, libraries, and models
  - Free Wide availability of necessary computing power to train models

- [https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4](https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4)

## The network

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- The neural network is "just" a function ${\text{NN}}_{ \theta }$:
  - Maps ${\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{D}} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{L}}$
  - Depends on a lot of parameters, $ \theta $.
- Construct a "complicated" function by chaining together many simpler functions:
  - $${\text{NN}}_{ \theta }={f}_{ \theta }^{(L)} \circ {f}_{ \theta }^{(L-1)} \circ ... \circ {f}_{ \theta }^{(2)} \circ {f}_{ \theta }^{(1)}$$
  - ${f}^{(1)}:{\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{D}} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{{h}_{1}}$, where ${h}_{1}$ is the width of the first "hidden layer"
  - Similarly, ${f}^{(j)}:{\mathbb{R}}^{{h}_{j-1}} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{{h}_{j}}$ for $j=2,...,L-1$
  - Finally, ${f}^{(L)}:{\mathbb{R}}^{{h}_{L-1}} \rightarrow {\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{L}}$
- Dimensions ${h}_{j}$ are "hyperparameters" of model (describe shape of network).

- [https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4](https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4)

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide17_pasted-movie.png){fig-alt="Diagram of a neural network with an input layer (six nodes, bracketed 'input layer'), two hidden layers (four and three nodes, bracketed 'hidden layers'), and a single-node output layer (bracketed 'output layer'), all connected by arrows, feeding into a final output arrow."}

- Example neural network
- $${\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{D}}$$
- $${f}^{(1)}$$
- $${f}^{(2)}$$
- $${\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{L}}$$
- $${f}^{(L)}$$

## The ${f}_{ \theta }^{(j)}$

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

- $${\text{NN}}_{ \theta }={f}_{ \theta }^{(L)} \circ {f}_{ \theta }^{(L-1)} \circ ... \circ {f}_{ \theta }^{(2)} \circ {f}_{ \theta }^{(1)}$$
- The ${f}^{(j)}$ are the basic units of the NN
  - They should be simple, but not too simple.
  - Specifically, they must be nonlinear!
  - Otherwise, the whole network reduces to a simple matrix operation, and nothing interesting happens.

- [https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html](https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html)

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide18_pasted-movie.png){fig-alt="Diagram of a neural network with an input layer (six nodes, bracketed 'input layer'), two hidden layers (four and three nodes, bracketed 'hidden layers'), and a single-node output layer (bracketed 'output layer'), all connected by arrows, feeding into a final output arrow."}

- Example neural network
- $${\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{D}}$$
- $${f}^{(1)}$$
- $${f}^{(2)}$$
- $${\mathbb{R}}^{{N}_{L}}$$
- $${f}^{(L)}$$
- [Directed, acyclic graph (DAG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directed_acyclic_graph)

- Building the network

- Sigmoid activation function:
  - $$ \sigma (x)=\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-x}}$$

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide22_pasted-movie.png){fig-alt="Plot of the sigmoid function, an S-shaped curve rising smoothly from 0 to 1 as its input goes from -6 to 6, crossing 0.5 at input 0."}

- Sigmoid function ([wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmoid_function))
- ReLU activation function:
  - $$max(x,0)$$

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide22_image19.png){fig-alt="Plot titled 'ReLU Activation Function': ReLU(x) is flat at 0 for x less than 0, then rises linearly with slope 1 for x greater than 0, shown over the range -10 to 10."}

- ReLU function ([https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/relu-activation-function-in-deep-learning/](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/deep-learning/relu-activation-function-in-deep-learning/))
- $$f(\text{y})= \phi \left( \mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{ \beta =1}}\limits^{{N}_{in}}{w}_{ \alpha  \beta }{y}_{ \beta }+{b}_{ \alpha } \right)$$

- Your activation function here

## Slide 33

- Function approximation

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

- So far, the network architecture may have seemed somewhat arbitrary.
- A vital reason NNs are so useful are formally described in universal approximation theorems: NNs can (in principle) approximate any continuous function!
- For example: for a feedforward NN with a single hidden layer, if the activation function is non-polynomial (e.g. sigmoid, ReLU), then the network can act as a "universal approximator."
  - [G. Cybenko, Approximation by superpositions of a sigmoidal function (1989)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02551274)
- Note: this is only a statement of existence! Existence does not help you make a good neural network, only that one exists :)

# Training

---

## Neural network training

- So, what about the "learning" part of "machine learning"?
- Training is the process of setting the weights in a NN for a given goal.
  - We've already done this a lot in CompPhys: least squares fitting, BFGS, etc.!
  - But now, we are dealing with >(>) thousands of parameters and input samples.
- A few broad categories:
  - Supervised
  - Unsupervised
  - Partially supervised
  - Reinforcement learning
- We will focus on supervised learning for today.

## Cost function

- The basis of training is the minimization of a cost function.
  - Remember back to fitting: we minimized the ${ \chi }^{2}$ of the data w.r.t. the fit function (with Newton, BFGS, etc.)
- As with fitting, for supervised learning, we have a well-defined target for each input sample, say $F({y}^{\text{in}})$, and we want to find the optimal weights, $w$, such that ${F}_{w}({y}^{\text{in}}) \approx F({y}^{\text{in}})$.
- A common cost function: "L2" norm (looks a lot like a ${ \chi }^{2}$):
- $$C(w)=\frac{1}{2}⟨ \parallel {F}_{w}({y}^{\text{in}}-F({y}^{\text{in}}){ \parallel }^{2}⟩$$
- Like neuron activation functions, there's some choice here:
  - "L1" norm, aka absolute value
  - Modify to penalize specific behavior (e.g. unwanted correlations)

![Screenshot 2025-10-01 at 12.38.24 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2025-10-01-at-12.38.24-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Table comparing four ways to encode the decimal numbers 0-7: Binary (3-bit), Unary (8-bit, filled left-to-right with 1s), and One-hot (8-bit, single 1 at the position matching the value)."}

- Fitting cosmological expansion

## Cost function

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- What about classification?
  - For regression, the output is a real number, so ${ \chi }^{2}$ makes sense
  - For classification, the output in discrete... how do we adapt for discrete math?
- First, define the output of the neural network: [one-hot encoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-hot)
  - For $N$ categories, output is a vector of length $N$
  - Each slot is 0 or 1, corresponding to the $N$ categories.
  - In practice, this works better than encoding categories as, e.g., a single integer (0–7); avoids assigning unwanted "meaning" to the output.

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide68_Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-12.08.17-PM.png){fig-alt="Table comparing four ways to encode the decimal numbers 0-7: Binary (3-bit), Unary (8-bit, filled left-to-right with 1s), and One-hot (8-bit, single 1 at the position matching the value)."}

- One-hot encoding
- True

- NN output

- Interpretation: "probability" that sample is in each category

---

## Cost function

- Popular loss function for categorical data: binary cross entropy, or log loss:
- $$\text{BCE}=-\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{i=1}}\limits^{N}\left[ {y}_{i}log({p}_{i})+(1-{y}_{i})log(1-{p}_{i}) \right]$$
- Go through a few cases to convince yourself (e.g. large number for incorrect ${p}_{i}$, zero for correct ${p}_{i}$):
  - ${y}_{0}=1$ and ${p}_{0}=1$?     $-1ln1=0$
  - ${y}_{0}=1$ and ${p}_{0}=0$?     $-1ln0= \infty $
  - ${y}_{0}=0$ and ${p}_{0}= \epsilon $?    $-0ln \epsilon =0$

- True

- NN output

---

## Minimizing the cost function

- Next, we minimize the cost function, $C(w)$, versus the weights $w$.
- We already know a lot about minimization... but now we have a huge number of parameters!
  - In other words, minimization over a huge dimensional space.
- Strategy:
  - Use some randomness (aka stochastic methods) to avoid local minima.
  - Use a relatively simple minimizer (we will have a lot of function calls, so they have to be cheap. No 2nd derivatives!)

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide70_image56.png){width="70%" fig-alt="3D rendered rugged landscape/terrain with red plateaus at the rim, orange-brown ridges, and a deep blue-white basin riddled with sharp jagged peaks and crevices at the bottom - illustrating a highly non-convex cost-function surface with many local minima."}

- A two dimensional section through the cost function (“loss landscape”) of a neural network from Li et al. (2018).
- [https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html](https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html)

## Gradient descent

## Gradient descent

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image57.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram titled 'Method: 'Sliding down the hill' ('gradient descent')': the formula w-dot ~ -grad_w C(w) above a plot of a cost function C(w) with two local minima, a red ball on the steep right slope with an arrow pointing downhill, and a note that a physicist would call this the motion of an overdamped particle."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- $${w}_{j} \rightarrow {w}_{j}- \eta \frac{ \partial C(w)}{ \partial {w}_{j}}$$

---

## Gradient descent

- The learning rate, $ \eta $, is another configurable handle on the algorithm:
  - Too large? Taylor expansion is not valid for large steps, so the step will be bad (increase $C(w)$).
  - Too small? Training will take a long time.
- Popular choice: start with large $ \eta $, but shrink over time (learning rate schedule).
  - Similar to the simulated annealing algorithm we studied last week.

- $${w}_{j} \rightarrow {w}_{j}- \eta \frac{ \partial C(w)}{ \partial {w}_{j}}$$

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide73_image58.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Figure comparing learning rates: four small plots show a ball's trajectory down a bowl-shaped loss curve for 'Learning rate too low' (slow, smooth), 'Good learning rate' (smooth convergence), 'High learning rate' (oscillating but converging), and 'Learning rate much too high' (diverging); below, a plot of loss L(w) versus training epoch for each case shows the 'much too high' rate diverging upward while the others decrease at different speeds."}

- https://www.bdhammel.com/learning-rates/

---

## Stochastic gradient descent

- Next, we minimize the cost function, $C(w)$, versus the weights $w$.
- We already know a lot about minimization... but now we have a huge number of parameters!
  - In other words, minimization over a huge dimensional space.
- Strategy:
  - Use some randomness (aka stochastic methods) to avoid local minima.
  - Use a relatively simple minimizer (we will have a lot of function calls, so they have to be cheap. No 2nd derivatives!)

---

## Stochastic gradient descent

- Training datasets are (ideally) very large: millions/billions of images
- Solution: train in batches, only using a fraction of the data for each gradient step.
  - The splitting and sampling is another configurable choice in your training.
  - So: ${w}_{j} \rightarrow {w}_{j}- \eta \frac{ \partial \mathop{C}\limits^{˜}(w)}{ \partial {w}_{j}}$, where $\mathop{C}\limits^{˜}(w)$ is the approximate cost function from a batch.
- Besides speedup, this actually improves the training (avoids local minima, reduces overfitting).

- $$C(w)=\frac{1}{2}⟨ \parallel {F}_{w}({y}^{\text{in}}-F({y}^{\text{in}}){ \parallel }^{2}⟩=\frac{1}{2N}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{i=1}}\limits^{N} \parallel {F}_{w}({y}^{\text{in}}-F({y}^{\text{in}}){ \parallel }^{2}$$

---

## Stochastic gradient descent

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image59.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram illustrating stochastic gradient descent: concentric blue contour rings (labeled 'C large' at center, 'C smaller' outward) with a jagged red zigzag path (labeled 'Stochastic gradient descent') descending toward the center, closely tracking a smooth straight yellow arrow (labeled 'True gradient of C'), with a note that for sufficiently small steps, the sum over many noisy steps approximates the true gradient."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

## Chain rule

- The final piece we need is the derivatives: computing all the $\frac{ \partial C(w)}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$ (${w}_{*}$=some ${w}_{ij}$ or ${b}_{j}$).
- Numerical differentiation is not going to work for billions of weights!
- Remember, the neural network is built by composing many simple functions, $NN={f}^{(N)} \circ {f}^{(N-1)} \circ ... \circ {f}^{(2)} \circ {f}^{(1)}(\mathbf{x})$
- So: we "just" need the chain rule
  - And a lot of bookkeeping!

![Screenshot 2026-03-09 at 1.14.43 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.14.43-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a multi-layer network of blue circular nodes connected by gray lines, with one connection near the bottom highlighted in red/orange and labeled w_* - illustrating a specific weight to be analyzed via the chain rule."}

- One weight in the neural network

---

## Simple example

- Let's look again at the smallest NN: two inputs, one output, no hidden layers:
  - Remember, $z={w}_{1}{y}_{1}+{w}_{2}{y}_{2}+b$
  - Output is $f(z)$, where $f$=RELU, sigmoid, tanh, ..
- Use the chain rule:
- $$\begin{matrix}
C(w) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨(f(x)-F({y}_{1},{y}_{2}){)}^{2}⟩ \\
\frac{ \partial C}{ \partial {w}_{1}} & =⟨(f(z)-F){f}^{′}(z)\frac{ \partial z}{ \partial {w}_{1}}⟩ \\
\frac{ \partial z}{ \partial {w}_{1}} & ={y}_{1} \\
\frac{ \partial C}{ \partial {w}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{i=1}}\limits^{N}(f({z}_{i})-{F}_{i}){f}^{′}({z}_{i}){y}_{1i}
\end{matrix}$$

![Screenshot 2026-03-09 at 1.16.05 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.16.05-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Small diagram labeled OUTPUT f(z) and INPUT y1, y2, showing a single output neuron connected to two input neurons, with additional text cut off at the right edge (likely a cost function C)."}

- Smallest unit of neural network
- (Expand average into sum over training samples)

---

## Full network

- For the full network, we need to roll up our sleeves and do the bookkeeping of indices.
  - ${y}_{j}^{(n)}$=value of neuron $j$ in layer $n$
  - ${z}_{j}^{(n)}$=input value for "$y=f(z)$"
    - So, ${y}_{j}^{(n)}=f({z}_{j}^{(n)})$
  - ${w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}$=weight for (neuron $k$ in layer $n-1$, feeding into neuron $j$ in layer $n$)
    - Similarly, ${b}_{j}^{n,n-1}$ for biases (might be omitted/left implicit in "$w$", just remember they are there).

![Screenshot 2026-03-09 at 1.14.43 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.14.43-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a multi-layer network of blue circular nodes connected by gray lines, with one connection near the bottom highlighted in red/orange and labeled w_* - illustrating a specific weight to be analyzed via the chain rule."}

- One weight in the neural network

---

## Full network

- Now, use the chain rule to step backwards through the network until we reach ${w}_{*}$.
  - Leave the average implicit, just calculate for one sample here.
- From output layer (${L}_{N}$) to ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$

![Screenshot 2026-03-09 at 1.14.43 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.14.43-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a multi-layer network of blue circular nodes connected by gray lines, with one connection near the bottom highlighted in red/orange and labeled w_* - illustrating a specific weight to be analyzed via the chain rule."}

- One weight in the neural network

---

## Full network

- Now, use the chain rule to step backwards through the network until we reach ${w}_{*}$.
  - Leave the average implicit, just calculate for one sample here.
- From output layer (${L}_{N}$) to ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {y}_{k}^{(n-1)}}\frac{ \partial {y}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$

![Screenshot 2026-03-09 at 1.14.43 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.14.43-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a multi-layer network of blue circular nodes connected by gray lines, with one connection near the bottom highlighted in red/orange and labeled w_* - illustrating a specific weight to be analyzed via the chain rule."}

- One weight in the neural network
- ..and so on until ${z}_{k}^{m}$ depends directly on ${w}_{*}$

---

## Backpropagation

- Key feature of backpropagation: a lot of the derivatives are reused many times.
- So, with some clever bookkeeping, we can reduce the computations significantly (i.e., we can reduce the order of the algorithm):
- $$\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$$
- We can save these values into a matrix, connecting layer ${L}_{N}$ to layer ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $${M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}={w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})$$

![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image62.png){width="70%" fig-alt="A thin, mostly empty orange-outlined rectangular border/frame."}

---

## Backpropagation

- Key feature of backpropagation: a lot of the derivatives are reused many times.
- So, with some clever bookkeeping, we can reduce the computations significantly (i.e., we can reduce the order of the algorithm):
- $$\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$$
- We can save these values into a matrix, connecting layer ${L}_{N}$ to layer ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $${M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}={w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})$$
- Going back several layers looks like:
- $$\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k,l,...,u,v}{M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{M}_{kl}^{(n-1,n-2)}...{M}_{uv}^{m+1,m}\frac{ \partial {z}_{v}^{(m)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$$

![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image62.png){width="70%" fig-alt="A thin, mostly empty orange-outlined rectangular border/frame."}

---

## Backpropagation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- $$\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k,l,...,u,v}{M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{M}_{kl}^{(n-1,n-2)}...{M}_{uv}^{m+1,m}\frac{ \partial {z}_{v}^{(m)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$$
- When we reach the layer that ${w}_{*}$ is in:
  - If ${w}_{*}$ is a weight, $\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(m)}}{ \partial {w}_{jk}^{m,m-1}}={y}_{k}^{(m-1)}$
  - If ${w}_{*}$ is a bias, $\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(m)}}{ \partial {b}_{j}^{m}}=1$

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide84_Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.14.43-PM.png){fig-alt="Diagram of a multi-layer network of blue circular nodes connected by gray lines, with one connection near the bottom highlighted in red/orange and labeled w_* - illustrating a specific weight to be analyzed via the chain rule."}

- One weight in the neural network

- $${L}_{N}$$

## Backpropagation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- A key point: each step back corresponds to a vector-matrix multiplication. Not matrix-matrix!
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$
- Pro: a naive computation (for example, "forward accumulation") might involve matrix-matrix computations at each stage.
- Con: have to store all the $M$ matrices.

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide85_Screenshot-2026-03-09-at-1.14.43-PM.png){fig-alt="Diagram of a multi-layer network of blue circular nodes connected by gray lines, with one connection near the bottom highlighted in red/orange and labeled w_* - illustrating a specific weight to be analyzed via the chain rule."}

- One weight in the neural network
- $${L}_{m}$$

- $${L}_{N}$$

- $${L}_{N-1}$$

- $$ \vdots $$

## Backpropagation

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- A key point: each step back corresponds to a vector-matrix multiplication. Not matrix-matrix!
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$
- Pro: a naive computation (for example, "forward accumulation") might involve matrix-matrix computations at each stage.
- Con: have to store all the $M$ matrices.
- Pro: in a single backpropagation pass, we can store all the ${z}_{j}^{(m)}$ and the ${f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(m)})$!

## Backpropagation

- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\

\end{matrix}$$

## Backpropagation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$
- Start with a vector corresponding to the first step of the chain rule:
- $${ \Delta }_{j}=({y}_{j}^{n}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{n})$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image71.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty pink/magenta rectangular border/frame."}
:::
::::

---

## Backpropagation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$
- Save (weight*derivative) as a matrix, connecting layer ${L}_{N}$ to layer ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $${M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}={w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})$$
- Start with a vector corresponding to the first step of the chain rule:
- $${ \Delta }_{j}=({y}_{j}^{n}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{n})$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image72.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty orange rectangular border/frame."}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image71.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty pink/magenta rectangular border/frame."}
:::
::::

---

## Backpropagation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$
- Save (weight*derivative) as a matrix, connecting layer ${L}_{N}$ to layer ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $${M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}={w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})$$
- The full chain rule equation is:
- $$\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k,l,...,u,v}{M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{M}_{kl}^{(n-1,n-2)}...{M}_{uv}^{m+1,m}\frac{ \partial {z}_{v}^{(m)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$$
- Each $\frac{ \partial C}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$ is obtained from a series of vector-matrix multiplications
  - Terminate upon reaching desired weight: $\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}}={y}_{k}^{(n-1)},\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {b}_{j}^{n}}=1$
- Start with a vector corresponding to the first step of the chain rule:
- $${ \Delta }_{j}=({y}_{j}^{n}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{n})$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image72.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty orange rectangular border/frame."}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image71.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty pink/magenta rectangular border/frame."}
:::
::::

## Overfitting

- A critical practical consideration: overfitting
- A model with too many parameters can just "memorize" the input data
  - Fails to learn the actual underlying model.
  - Poor generalization when applied beyond training dataset.

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide121_image90.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Scatter plot of red and blue data points with a smooth black curve (the true decision boundary) and a jagged green curve weaving tightly between individual points - illustrating an overfit classifier boundary that follows noise rather than the true underlying trend."}

- Overfitting (wikipedia)
- [https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4](https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4)

---

## Overfitting

- A critical practical consideration: overfitting
- A model with too many parameters can just "memorize" the input data
  - Fails to learn the actual underlying model.
  - Poor generalization when applied beyond training dataset.
- Example: [Zhang 2021](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3446776)
  - Trained computer vision models on randomly labelled images
  - Perfect performance on training data, random guessing on testing data!

- [https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4](https://computational-physics.tripos.org/slides/autodiff.html#/0/4)

- Overfitting (wikipedia)

## Overfitting

![Screenshot 2026-03-11 at 1.05.22 PM.png](../assets/6.0_ml/Screenshot-2026-03-11-at-1.05.22-PM.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a dataset split into a Validation set (5000 images, light green, 'never used for training, but used during training for assessing accuracy'), a Training set (45000 images, dark green, 'used for training'), and a separate Test set (10000 images, orange, 'never used during training, only later to test fully trained net'), with a note that these numbers are for the MNIST example."}

- Division into training, validation, and set data sets
- Use validation set to judge performance during training
  - Termination criteria: stop when validation accuracy stops improving
- Switch out training data (batching strategy); add some noise
- "Dropout": randomly 0 out neurons during training (also noise)

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

## Example: pytorch

- device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator().type if torch.accelerator.is_available() else "cpu"
- class NeuralNetwork(nn.Module):
- def __init__(self):
- super().__init__()
- self.flatten = nn.Flatten()
- self.linear_relu_stack = nn.Sequential(
- nn.Linear(28*28, 512),
- nn.ReLU(),
- nn.Linear(512, 512),
- nn.ReLU(),
- nn.Linear(512, 10)
- )
- def forward(self, x):
- x = self.flatten(x)
- logits = self.linear_relu_stack(x)
- return logits
- model = NeuralNetwork().to(device)
- print(model)

- loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
- optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
- def train_loop(dataloader, model, loss_fn, optimizer):
- size = len(dataloader.dataset)
- model.train() # set mode
- for batch, (X, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
- # Compute prediction and loss
- pred = model(X)
- loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
- # Backpropagation
- loss.backward()
- optimizer.step()
- optimizer.zero_grad()
- epochs = 10
- for t in range(epochs):
- train_loop(train_dataloader, model, loss_fn, optimizer)
- test_loop(test_dataloader, model, loss_fn)
- print("Done!")

## Example: flax

- import flax
- from flax import linen as nn
- # Use FLAX for research and experimental projects
- class MyModel(nn.Module):
- hidden_dim: int
- def setup(self):
- self.dense = nn.Dense(self.hidden_dim)
- self.output = nn.Dense(10)
- def __call__(self, inputs):
- x = nn.relu(self.dense(inputs))
- return self.output(x)
- model = MyModel(hidden_dim=64)
- # Train and evaluate the model
- optimizer = flax.optim.Adam(learning_rate=0.001).create(model)
- for batch in dataset:
- optimizer = optimizer.train_step(batch)

## Last time: feed forward

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- original version: Haade;vectorization: Wjh31, Quibik, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

![](../assets/6.0_ml/slide139_image26.png){fig-alt="The same feedforward-pass diagram, further along in the walkthrough: the first hidden layer is now fully computed and values are appearing in the second hidden layer (0.5, 0.2, -2.3, ...) as the computation propagates forward."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- ${y}_{j}^{(n)}$ = value of neurons in $n$th layer

- ${w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}$ = weights (layer $n-1$ to $n$)

- ${z}_{j}^{(n)}$=input for "$y=f(z)$"
- =${w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{y}_{k}^{(n-1)}+{b}_{j}^{n,n-1}$

## Last time: backpropagation

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image69.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram titled 'Backpropagation: the principle': the full chain-rule path from a red C (cost) node down through three black f'(z) nodes (each connected by an edge labeled w) to the red-highlighted w_* connection at the bottom, labeled y and w_* - showing every factor in the chain rule from w_* to C. Annotated 'and now: sum over ALL possible paths!' and 'efficient implementation: repeated matrix/vector multiplication'."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

## Last time: backpropagation

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- $$\begin{matrix}
\frac{ \partial C(w,{y}^{\text{in}})}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}}))\frac{ \partial {y}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
 & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j \in {L}_{N}}({y}_{j}^{(n)}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{(n)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} \\
\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}} & =\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k \in {L}_{N-1}}{w}_{jk}^{n,n-1}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})\frac{ \partial {z}_{k}^{(n-1)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}
\end{matrix}$$
- Save (weight*derivative) as a matrix, connecting layer ${L}_{N}$ to layer ${L}_{N-1}$:
- $${M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}={w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{f}^{′}({z}_{k}^{(n-1)})$$
- The full chain rule equation is:
- $$\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k,l,...,u,v}{M}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}{M}_{kl}^{(n-1,n-2)}...{M}_{uv}^{m+1,m}\frac{ \partial {z}_{v}^{(m)}}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$$
- Each $\frac{ \partial C}{ \partial {w}_{*}}$ is obtained from a series of vector-matrix multiplications
  - Terminate upon reaching desired weight: $\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {w}_{jk}^{(n,n-1)}}={y}_{k}^{(n-1)},\frac{ \partial {z}_{j}^{(n)}}{ \partial {b}_{j}^{n}}=1$
- Start with a vector corresponding to the first step of the chain rule:
- $${ \Delta }_{j}=({y}_{j}^{n}-{F}_{j}({y}^{\text{in}})){f}^{′}({z}_{j}^{n})$$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image72.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty orange rectangular border/frame."}
![Rectangle Rectangle](../assets/6.0_ml/image71.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Thin, mostly empty pink/magenta rectangular border/frame."}
:::

## Types of neural networks

- The networks so far are multilayer perceptrons, built from fully connected layers.
  - These can already do a lot of interesting things, e.g. the universal approximation theorem.
- But! The universal approximation theorem is a statement of existence, not efficiency!
  - Fully connected layers are somewhat expensive (${N}_{j-1} \times {N}_{j}$ weights)

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide143_image98.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a dense feedforward network with unlabeled nodes: an Input Layer in R^16 (16 nodes), two Hidden Layers in R^12 and R^10, and an Output Layer in R^1 (1 node), with every node in each layer connected to every node in the next."}

- [https://towardsdatascience.com/classifying-handwritten-digits-using-a-multilayer-perceptron-classifier-mlp-bc8453655880/](https://towardsdatascience.com/classifying-handwritten-digits-using-a-multilayer-perceptron-classifier-mlp-bc8453655880/)

---

## Types of neural networks

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- In practice, you can do a lot better if the neural network's structure mirrors the problem/data structure.
  - Convolutional NNs: scan a small "filter" over an image to extract local features (e.g. edges).
  - Recurrent NNs: parse sequential data (e.g. time series, sentences) with built-in "memory" that remembers recent inputs
  - Autoencoders: NN has a "bottleneck", forcing NN to focus on most important features
  - Graph NNs: inputs have a graph structure (e.g. molecules, point-cloud camera data, LHC jet constituents) with permutation-invariant nodes and edges
  - Transformers: [Attention Is All You Need](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_Is_All_You_Need)
  - ...

- [https://nl.mathworks.com/discovery/convolutional-neural-network.html](https://nl.mathworks.com/discovery/convolutional-neural-network.html)

## Types of neural networks

- Recall: the universal approximation theorem is a statement of existence, not efficiency!
  - Fully connected layers are somewhat expensive (${N}_{j-1} \times {N}_{j}$ weights)
- In practice, a neural network's structure can be constructed to mirror the geometry of the problem.
  - Convolutional NNs: scan a small "filter" over an image to extract local features (e.g. edges).
  - Recurrent NNs: parse sequential data (e.g. time series, sentences) with built-in "memory" that remembers recent inputs
  - Autoencoders: NN has a "bottleneck", forcing NN to focus on most important features
  - Graph NNs: inputs have a graph structure (e.g. molecules, point-cloud camera data, LHC jet constituents) with permutation-invariant nodes and edges
  - ...

## Soft-max activation function

- Output probabilities are generated by the softmax activation function
- $${f}_{j}({z}_{1},{z}_{2},...)=\frac{{e}^{{z}_{j}}}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} {{e}^{{z}_{k}}}}$$
  - The final set of ${z}_{j}$ are called logits ("raw scores")
  - Multi-variable generalization of the sigmoid, $f(x)=\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-x}}$

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image107.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of MNIST digit classification with soft outputs: the same 28x28 input image of a handwritten '6' feeds through the network to ten output nodes labeled 0-9, now showing probability values (.1, 0, 0, 0, .1, .1, .7, 0, 0, 0) with node 6 highlighted red as the largest (.7), captioned 'output: probabilities (select largest)'."}

- Softmax activation

## Binary cross-entropy

- Loss categorical data: binary cross entropy, or log loss:
- $$\text{BCE}=-\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{i=1}}\limits^{N}\left[ {y}_{i}log({p}_{i})+(1-{y}_{i})log(1-{p}_{i}) \right]$$
- Go through a few cases to convince yourself:
  - ${y}_{0}=1$ and ${p}_{0}=1- \epsilon $?     $-(1ln(1- \epsilon )+0ln( \epsilon ))=0$
  - ${y}_{0}=0$ and ${p}_{0}=0+ \epsilon $?    $-(0ln( \epsilon )+1ln(1- \epsilon ))=0$
  - ${y}_{0}=1$ and ${p}_{0}=0+ \epsilon $?     $-(1ln \epsilon +0ln(1- \epsilon )) \rightarrow  \infty $
- Inspired by entropy: $S=-\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}{p}_{j}ln{p}_{j}$
  - Non-negative, additive for factorizable distributions
  - Connected to maximum likelihood

- True (${y}_{i}$)

- NN output (${p}_{i}$)

---

## Binary cross-entropy

- Loss categorical data: binary cross entropy, or log loss:
- $$\text{BCE}=-\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{i=1}}\limits^{N}\left[ {y}_{i}log({p}_{i})+(1-{y}_{i})log(1-{p}_{i}) \right]$$
- Go through a few cases to convince yourself:
  - ${y}_{0}=1$ and ${p}_{0}=1- \epsilon $?     $-(1ln(1- \epsilon )+0ln( \epsilon ))=0$
  - ${y}_{0}=0$ and ${p}_{0}=0+ \epsilon $?    $-(0ln( \epsilon )+1ln(1- \epsilon ))=0$
  - ${y}_{0}=1$ and ${p}_{0}=0+ \epsilon $?     $-(1ln \epsilon +0ln(1- \epsilon )) \rightarrow  \infty $
- Inspired by entropy: $S=-\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}{p}_{j}ln{p}_{j}$
  - Non-negative, additive for factorizable distributions
  - Connected to [maximum likelihood estimation](https://leimao.github.io/blog/Cross-Entropy-KL-Divergence-MLE/)

- True (${y}_{i}$)

- NN output (${p}_{i}$)

# Convolutional neural networks

---

## Convolutions

- Remember the definition of a convolution from last semester:
  - Continuous: $(f*g)(x)= \int f({x}^{′})g(x-{x}^{′})d{x}^{′}$
  - Discrete: $(f*g{)}_{i}=\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{g}_{i-j}$
  - Similarly for higher dimensions
- Convolution theorem: convolution in real space $ \Leftrightarrow $ multiplication in Fourier domain, and vice versa:
  - $F[f*g]=F[f]F[g]$, and ${F}^{-1}[\mathop{f}\limits^{˜}*\mathop{g}\limits^{˜}]={F}^{-1}[\mathop{f}\limits^{˜}]{F}^{-1}[\mathop{g}\limits^{˜}]$
  - Example: convolving with a Gaussian "smoothens out" a function;
    - In Fourier domain (remember, FT of a Gaussian is another Gaussian), this corresponds to multiplying the FT by a Gaussian; this suppresses higher-frequency modes.
- In physics, we see convolutions in the context of things like Green's functions and signal filtering.

---

## CNNs

- Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are intrinsically translation invariant:
  - The kernels learn some local feature
  - Since the CNN scans the kernel over the whole image, that feature is detected anywhere in the image!
- MUCH more memory-efficient than dense layers:
  - E.g. first dense layer has ${N}_{\text{pixels}} \times {N}_{\text{neurons}}$ weights
    - E.g. (28*28) * 256 =200,704 weights
  - Convolutional layer just has $M$ weights per feature (e.g. $M=9$ for a $3 \times 3$ kernel), which are reused many times during the scanning.
    - E.g. (3*3) * 32 =288

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image115.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide titled 'The convolutional filters': a row of seven small pixelated grayscale filter patches (each showing a distinct light/dark pattern); captioned 'Interpretation: try to extract common features of input images! 'diagonal line', 'curve bending towards upper right corner', etc.'."}

- Example of 7 CNN filters. These extract features like "diagonal line", "curve bending towards upper right", etc.

---

## CNNs: additional tools

- A simple convolutional layer applied to a $N \times N$ image will produce $ \approx N \times N$ values (minus a few, depending on how you handle the edges).
  - For most images, this is overkill!
    - Features are probably bigger than 3 pixels
    - Pixel-exact location of features is probably not important
  - [Pooling layers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pooling_layer) downsample the output of a convolutional layer, combining nearby pixels
    - Max, average are common choices
- [Batch normalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batch_normalization) rescales inputs to a layer to e.g. [-1, 1], preventing values from blowing up or shrinking.

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image4.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram titled 'Single depth slice': a 4x4 grid of numbers divided into four 2x2 colored quadrants (orange: 1,0,4,6; green: 2,3,6,8; blue: 3,1,1,2; gray: 1,0,2,4), with an arrow showing max-pooling reducing it to a 2x2 grid (6, 8, 3, 4 - the max of each quadrant)."}

- Pooling layer with max function

---

## CNNs: all together now

- In total, a simple CNN might contain:
  - Convolutional layer: discern features
  - Pooling layer: extract global features
  - Activation function (e.g. relu)
  - (Repeat)
  - Fully connected layer(s)
  - Loss layer: softmax maps raw outputs to "probabilities"

## Clustering algorithms

- Popular clustering algorithms:
  - $k$-means
    - Partition into k clusters using mean central values (usually exclusively)
  - Agglomerative hierarchical clustering
    - Pair individual elements into clusters given some distance metric
  - Density based scan (DBSCAN)
    - Considers low-density regions to be noise
    - Not exclusive clustering
    - See: Dr. Martin Kwok's [colloquium](https://indico.fnal.gov/event/68002/contributions/308390/attachments/186176/256468/MDS_WineAndCheese_v4.pdf) from last semester (long-lived particle search using muon detector showers)

---

## $k$-means algorithm

- Algorithm 8.1 Basic $k$-means algorithm
  - Select $k$ points as initial centroids
  - REPEAT:
    - Form $k$ clusters by assigning each point to the nearest centroid
    - Recompute centroid of each cluster
  - UNTIL:
    - Centroids do not change

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image121.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Four-panel figure titled illustrating k-means algorithm iterations: scattered triangle, square, and circle markers with three '+' centroid markers repositioning across Iteration 1 through Iteration 4, converging toward the center of each natural group of points."}

- Cartoon of k-means clustering algorithm

---

## $k$-means algorithm

- What is $k$-means computing?
  - Formally, consider the following RMS:
  - $${\text{RMS}}^{2}=\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{i=1}}\limits^{k}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{j=1}}\limits^{n}|{\vec{c}}_{i}-{\vec{x}}_{j}{|}^{2}$$
  - Minimize the RMS by adjusting the centroids
  - Note: can use other distance metrics besides Euclidean
- The computational complexity of $k$-means is $ \approx $linear in the sum of:
  - Number of points
  - Number of dimensions (=attributes)
  - Number of clusters
  - Number of iterations to converge

---

## Bisecting $k$-means

- Shortcomings of basic $k$-means:
  - As with all iterative minimization routines, watch out for local minima (need heuristic methods to avoid getting trapped)
  - Can produce empty clusters if initialized poorly!
  - Very sensitive to outliers
- Bisecting $k$-means mitigates the "cons" by splitting and merging clusters:
- Initialize list of clusters to [cluster containing all points]
- do:
  - Choose random cluster from the list of clusters
  - for i in range(n_trials):
    - Bisect selected cluster using $k$-means
    - Compute RMS of bisected cluster
  - Choose pair of smaller clusters with lowest RMS
  - Replace original cluster with pair of smaller clusters
- until we have $k$ clusters

---

## Voronoi diagrams

- The result of $k$-means is a [Voronoi diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voronoi_diagram)
  - Given a set of centroids (points), partition space into regions corresponding to (closest to a given point)
- "Cachement areas": from river basins, water tables, etc... where does water pool when it rains?
- See CompPhys/DataScience/kmeans.ipynb for an example
  - Relevant for Midterm Problem 2!

## Hierarchical clustering

- Agglomerative clustering ("bottom up"):
  - Start with individual constituents, merge iteratively until termination condition
- Divise clustering ("top down"):
  - Start with everything, split iteratively until termination condition (e.g. reach individual constituents)
- Results can be represented by a tree-like structure (aka dendrogram) or a Venn diagram.

## Fastjet algorithm

- The famous FastJet algorithm reduces $O({N}^{3})$ to $O(NlnN)$.
  - Particle physicists think this is pretty cool, but computation geometers have studied this for much longer!
- Basic idea: instead of full $N \times N$ distance matrix, pre-compute a list of nearest neighbors for each point (length $N$).
  - Each step merges 2 points
  - We only have to check if the new point changes any nearest neighbors: $N$ operations
  - $$ \Rightarrow O({N}^{2})$$
- Further speedup: use Voronoi diagrams to find nearest neighbors (see [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-ph/0512210)) to get $O(NlnN)$.

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide185_image124.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Step-by-step diagram of the Fastjet clustering algorithm: starting from initial particles (dots of varying size representing momentum), the two closest particles (smallest d_ij) are repeatedly combined into larger 'protojets' (highlighted purple/black), continuing until d_ij > d_iB stops the clustering, ending with 4 found jets, each containing several original particles (shown color-coded by jet membership)."}

- Anti-${k}_{T}$ jet clustering algorithm

## Principal component analysis

- Last time: introduced autoencoders, NNs with a restricted layer (bottleneck or latent space).
  - Restricted layer force NN to learn only "important" features
- This is closely related to principal component analysis: a technique for determining the most important "axes" in a given dataset
  - In other words, identify the linear combinations of features with the most variance.
  - Often, you can reduce to the dimensionality of a dataset using only the top X% most interesting features.

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide191_image128.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Scatter plot of a cloud of correlated 2D data points (gray, roughly diagonal ellipse from bottom-left to top-right), with two black arrows from the cluster's center pointing along the two principal component directions (one along the main diagonal spread, one perpendicular to it)."}

- PCA of a multivariate Gaussian distribution centered at (1, 3) with a standard deviation of 3 in roughly the (0.866, 0.5) direction and of 1 in the orthogonal direction. The vectors shown are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix scaled by the square root of the corresponding eigenvalue, and shifted so their tails are at the mean.

## Principal component analysis

- Given a dataset with $N$ features,${{X}^{i}}$, and $m$ points:
  - Standardize each feature: scale to have mean ${\overline{x}}^{i}$=0 and $ \sigma =1$.
  - Compute covariance matrix:
- PCA is easy from here: PCs are just the eigenvectors of ${\text{cov}}_{ij}$, ranked by the eigenvalues!
  - Specifically: ${\text{cov}}_{ij}$ is real and symmetric, so we can write it as $ED{E}^{T}$, where $E$ is the eigenvector column matrix and $D$ is diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.
  - $E$ encodes a rotation to a basis where (a) the covariance matrix is diagonal, and (b) the variance of the new basis vectors is given by the eigenvalues in $D$.

- $${\text{cov}}_{ij}=\frac{1}{m-1}\mathop{\mathop{ \sum }\limits_{k=1}}\limits^{m}({x}_{k}^{i}-{\overline{x}}^{i})({X}_{k}^{j}-{\overline{x}}^{j})$$

- [https://cybernetist.com/2016/04/12/principal-component-analysis-part-2/](https://cybernetist.com/2016/04/12/principal-component-analysis-part-2/)

---

## AEs and PCA

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image133.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide titled 'Solution: Consider the matrix': defines rho-hat = <|psi><psi|> = sum_j p_j |psi^(j)><psi^(j)|, with rho_mn = <psi_m psi_n*>, noted as the covariance matrix of the vectors (compare density matrix in quantum physics); claims diagonalizing this Hermitian matrix and keeping the M eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues gives the desired set of 'v'."}

## t-SNE

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image145.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide titled ''Stochastic neighbor embedding' (SNE)': defines p_ij as the probability of picking a pair of points (i,j), larger for close neighbors in high-dimensional space, and q_ij as the analogous probability in low-dimensional space, with both normalized so sum_{i!=j} p_ij = sum_{i!=j} q_ij = 1."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

## t-SNE

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image145.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide titled ''Stochastic neighbor embedding' (SNE)': defines p_ij as the probability of picking a pair of points (i,j), larger for close neighbors in high-dimensional space, and q_ij as the analogous probability in low-dimensional space, with both normalized so sum_{i!=j} p_ij = sum_{i!=j} q_ij = 1."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- "The similarity of datapoint ${x}_{j}$ to datapoint ${x}_{j}$ is the conditional probability, ${p}_{j|i}$, that ${x}_{i}$ would pick ${x}_{j}$ as its neighbor if neighbors were picked in proportion to their probability density under a Gaussian centered at ${x}_{i}$."

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

## t-SNE

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image146.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide stating the SNE objective: want the q-distribution to closely approximate the p-distribution, formalized as the Kullback-Leibler divergence C = KL(P||Q) = sum_i sum_j p_ij log(p_ij/q_ij), a way of comparing probability distributions."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image146.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide stating the SNE objective: want the q-distribution to closely approximate the p-distribution, formalized as the Kullback-Leibler divergence C = KL(P||Q) = sum_i sum_j p_ij log(p_ij/q_ij), a way of comparing probability distributions."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- Adversarial training: penalize NN to "force" outputs to satisfy some desired condition, e.g., avoid sculpting jet mass distribution in jet tagging.

## t-SNE

![TODO: describe image](../assets/6.0_ml/image147.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Slide titled 'Choices made for t-SNE' (citing Hinton & van der Maaten 2008): in high-dimensional space, p_j|i is a Gaussian-based ratio exp(-||x_i-x_j||^2/2*sigma_i^2) normalized over k, combined into p_ij = (p_j|i + p_i|j)/2n; in low-dimensional space, q_ij uses a Cauchy/Student-t distribution (1+||y_i-y_j||^2)^-1 normalized over k,l - noted that q's heavier tails give low-dimensional points more room to spread out at intermediate distances."}

- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)
- [F. Marquardt, Machine Learning for Physicists 2024](https://pad.gwdg.de/s/ZwIoM-Arn)

## Recap

- Principal component analysis (PCA) is a dimensionality reduction algorithm that identifies orthogonal, linear combinations of features ranked by variance
  - Relatively simple: construct covariance matrix, compute eigenvectors/values
- Autoencoders with linear activations are basically just PCA!
- Visualizing the with latent space (e.g t-SNE) illustrates what the NN is doing
- Notebooks: machine-learning-for-physicsists/2024/05*tSNE*ipynb
- Further reading:
  - What if you chop the AE in half, and just take the decoder side?
  - Map from latent space to outputs: generative AI!
  - Uses a modified, probabilistic latent space layer: [variational AEs](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/variational-autoencoder)

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide221_image153.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a variational autoencoder (VAE): an Input Image (MNIST '2') feeds through an 'encode -> Inference' network to a latent bottleneck with mean (mu) and variance (sigma) parameters (q_phi(z|x)), sampling a Gaussian Latent Distribution, then through a 'decode -> Generative' network (p_theta(x|z)) to a Reconstructed Image (x-tilde, also a '2')."}

- Variational autoencoder
![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide221_image154.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of a basic autoencoder: an Input layer of six gray nodes (x1-x6) connects through an 'encoder' arrow to Hidden layers (narrowing from 4 to 3 blue nodes and back to 4), then through a 'decoder' arrow to an Output layer of six gray nodes (x-hat_1 to x-hat_6) - the classic bowtie/hourglass autoencoder shape."}

- Latent space visualization

## Last time

- Autoencoders aim to represent most important features of the data in a compressed "bottleneck" layer, called the latent space.
  - Encoder: maps inputs to latent space (compression, recognition)
  - Decoder: maps latent space to outputs (decompression, generation)
- Self-supervised problem: neural network learns to reproduce the data without any other specific goal.

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide224_image156.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Hand-drawn colorful infographic titled 'DEEP LEARNING BASICS LINK MAP' (F.M. 2021): colored boxes for Basic structure of neural networks (Lecture 1, Rosenblatt 58, Hinton review 89), Cost function and stochastic gradient descent / Backpropagation (Lecture 2, Hinton review 89, Linnainmaa 76, Rumelhart et al 85), Image recognition (Lecture 3), Convolutional neural networks (Lecture 4, Fukushima 80, LeCun et al 89, Krizhevsky et al 12), Autoencoders / Principal component analysis (Lecture 4, Baldi et al 89, Hinton et al 06, Bengio et al review 12), Other dimensionality-reducing techniques / t-SNE (Lecture 5, van der Maaten et al 08), Recurrent neural networks / LSTM / word vectors (Lectures 5-6, Hochreiter et al 95, Mikolov et al 13), Reinforcement learning (Lectures 6-8, Williams 92, Watkins et al 92), Boltzmann machine (Lecture 9, Sejnowski 85), plus references to lecture notes, books, and an online course."}

- Autoencoder

## Variational autoencoders

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide230_image160.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Full VAE diagram: an input layer x1-x6 feeds through two encoder hidden layers to a 'Define latent state distributions' stage producing Mean (mu1, mu2) and Variance (sigma1, sigma2) nodes; these are sampled to produce latent values z1, z2, which feed through two decoder hidden layers to an output layer x-hat_1 through x-hat_6."}

- Variational autoencoder
- Variational autoencoders have a probabilistic latent space: each input becomes a distribution in the latent space (e.g. Gaussian), not a single point.
  - Network learns both mean (${ \mu }_{i}$) and width (${ \sigma }_{i}$) for each latent space dimension
  - (Regular autoencoder: ${ \sigma }_{i}=0$)
- This forces the network to learn a smoother distribution in the latent space.

- [https://www.jeremyjordan.me/variational-autoencoders/](https://www.jeremyjordan.me/variational-autoencoders/)

---

## Variational autoencoders

- Caveat: how do you perform backpropagation through a random sampling layer?
- "Reparametrization trick": keep track of the randomness in a parameter $ \epsilon $, where $z= \mu + \sigma  \cdot  \epsilon $.
- $ \epsilon $ is sample from a normal gaussian ($ \mu =0$, $ \sigma =1$), no training needed.

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide231_image161.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Diagram of the VAE reparameterization trick: left, the latent node z (random, blue circle) sampled directly from q(z|x) given encoder outputs mu and sigma (deterministic, gray diamonds); right, after reparameterization, z is instead computed deterministically as z = mu + sigma (dot) epsilon, with epsilon drawn as a separate random node from N(0,1) - moving the randomness outside the network so gradients can flow through mu and sigma."}

- Reparametrization trick
- [https://www.jeremyjordan.me/variational-autoencoders/](https://www.jeremyjordan.me/variational-autoencoders/)

---

## Variational autoencoders

- Second ingredient: imposing a specific geometry on the latent space.
- The variational layer probably degrades the performance (i.e. the reconstruction loss)... so naively, we might expect the training to send ${ \sigma }_{i} \rightarrow 0$.
- Solution: add a penalty to the loss function with K–L divergence
  - Recall t-SNE: KL measures similarity between 2 probability distributions, $p(x)$ vs. $q(x)$
  - $${D}_{\text{KL}}(P \parallel Q)= \int p(x)log(p(x)/q(x))dx$$
  - Use KL penalty to force latent space to be (e.g.) a unit Gaussian in each dimension.

![pasted-movie.png](../assets/6.0_ml/slide232_image159.png){width="70%" fig-alt="Three scatter plots of a 2D latent space (points colored by MNIST digit 0-9): 'Only reconstruction loss' shows streaky, partially separated clusters with points labeled 1, 2, 7 near a boundary; 'Only KL divergence' shows one large unseparated blob; 'Combination' shows better-separated clusters, again with points labeled 1, 2 near a boundary region."}

- MNIST latent space with (left) reconstruction loss, (middle) KL divergence loss, and (right) combination of both losses
- [https://www.jeremyjordan.me/variational-autoencoders/](https://www.jeremyjordan.me/variational-autoencoders/)

## Recurrent neural networks

<!-- TODO: complex slide layout (flagged by detect_complex_slide.py - see run log). Content below is complete but UNARRANGED - needs manual layout to match the original slide. -->

- Recurrent: can "remember" (=save state) of inputs
  - CNNs do not!
- Example: predict the next value in a sequence
  - $ \Rightarrow $ clear applications to language processing
- Example: measure similarity of two sequences
- Key issue: vanishing gradients
  - =loss of long-term memory
  - Mitigations: long short-term memory (LSTM), gated recurrent units (GRUs).
- Still used today, but replaced by [transformers](https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/) in many applications
  - Key feature: instead of sequential processing, process full input (e.g. text query to ChatGPT) with attention mechanism to identify relevant combinations of inputs
